record: SPAC PAC endorsed her in the Ward 4 special election, and the 2026 report calls her "an active partner to the Chamber." Voted on every recorded 2026 vote and sided with the majority on 12 of 13 split votes. Spoke in favor of the drive-through ordinance (Ord 24-26). Appointed to the Workforce Innovation Board (Sept 2, 2026). Most active member on events and sound permits; also leads on land use.
approach: Make her the Chamber's first briefing and lead sponsor. Ask her to carry Chamber-drafted amendment language and to convene colleagues. Because she sits in the majority, she is the bridge to a fourth vote, starting with Johnson, the colleague she votes with most.
engage_on: Workforce and talent (Talent Hub, Drive for 5 retention and upskilling) through her Workforce Innovation Board seat; quality-of-life and hospitality items (events, downtown activity); land use and permitting.
lead_with: "Catalytic leadership drives progress" and "A strong business climate equals a strong community."
cautions: Do not make her the lone public face on contested items; she wins by building majorities. Keep the PAC relationship separate from official asks and follow city lobbying-disclosure rules.
chamber_relationship: SPAC PAC endorsement (Ward 4 special election), per the 2026 report

stance: Issue champion: regulation and land use
record: Carried the drive-through ordinance (Ord 24-26) through Versions 2 and 3 to a 7-0 adoption on March 4, 2026. Leads on utilities and fees, licensing, and zoning. Votes most like Noecker (69% of split votes). Has the most dissents (6) and sided with the majority on 7 of 13 split votes. Spoke to legal concerns on, and voted against, the tenant-repair ballot question. Voted against delaying the McMahon appointment.
approach: Treat him as the technical partner on regulatory fixes. Bring draft amendment language, cost data and peer-city comparisons early, before first reading. Pair him with Noecker, then add Coleman and Johnson to reach four.
engage_on: Drive-through and land-use rules, license and fee schedules (e.g., Ord 26-56 garbage rates and Ord 26-53 mobile sauna licensing on Nov 4), utility franchises.
lead_with: "Support an economic environment that promotes business growth": regulatory certainty, as in the Chamber's permitting-reform win.
cautions: He is often on the losing side of split votes, so his support alone does not carry a contested item. What the final drive-through ordinance allows is NOT AVAILABLE in the minutes; confirm against the ordinance text before claiming a win.

record: Council President. Leads on economic development and on appointments and council governance. Made the most motions to delay (8). Spoke in favor of the Galtier Plaza TIF district and the drive-through ordinance. Offered Version 3 of the pre-eviction notice ordinance (failed 2-5). Spoke in favor of the festival security credit and raised concerns on writing off police festival costs. Sided with the majority on 9 of 13 split votes.
approach: Brief her before any downtown or development item reaches the agenda. Delays usually come from her, and 15 of the 16 delayed items that later came back for a recorded vote were adopted, so resolve her questions in advance to avoid a layover. Bring fiscal and economic-impact data.
engage_on: Downtown revitalization (TIF, Galtier Plaza, the downtown special service district), economic-development appointments, budget and fiscal items.
lead_with: "Drive Progress": advocate for business growth and new economic-development opportunities.
cautions: She was in the minority on 4 of 13 split votes, so pair her support with majority members. Her procedural role (presiding, layovers) shapes timing more than outcomes.

record: Leads on housing and tenant rules. Moved the HRA Housing Trust Fund budget amendment (Feb 25, 2026), which six members, including Johnson, spoke for. Spoke in favor of the Galtier Plaza TIF district. Spoke to legal concerns on, and voted against, the tenant-repair ballot question. Sided with the majority on 11 of 12 split votes. Cast no votes in January and missed most of February's.
approach: Partner on housing production and access. Present the "CUB Tax Credit and Housing" priority as more homes and more workers housed near jobs. Coordinate with Coleman, the colleague she votes with most.
engage_on: Housing supply and financing (Housing Trust Fund, HOME-ARP, conduit housing bonds), downtown revitalization, workforce access.
lead_with: "Equity is the lens through which we do all our work" and the policy platform: people need access to employment and housing.
cautions: Confirm she will attend before a key vote; her early-year absences changed vote counts. On tenant protections she weighs legal risk closely, so bring legal analysis, not only economic arguments.

record: Vice President. Leads on housing and tenant rules and on political and social items. Moved the tenant-repair ballot question, which failed 2-5 with only Kim joining her. Spoke against extending the ForwardEdge grant (denied 0-6). Spoke in favor of the HRA Housing Trust Fund and the final drive-through ordinance. Voted the same way as Kim on all 12 split votes they both cast.
approach: Lead with listening rather than lobbying. Hold a "courageous conversation" meeting on her priorities, then look for overlap: workforce equity, BIPOC and small-business growth, and more housing. Offer joint employer-tenant solutions instead of opposing her proposals outright.
engage_on: Workforce and equity programs, small-business support, housing production, Housing Trust Fund.
lead_with: "Courageous, deep listening effects change" and "Equity is the lens through which we do all our work."
cautions: Expect different views on landlord and tenant regulation and on business incentives without community-benefit terms. She and Kim move together, so engage both. Her positions on most Chamber priorities are NOT AVAILABLE from the minutes beyond these votes.

record: Voted the same way as Yang on all 12 split votes they both cast. Moved denial of the ForwardEdge grant extension (denied 0-6), moved approval of the Baillon Company rezoning and a Seventh Place Mall final order, and moved the resolution urging divestment from companies that enable ICE (later laid over). Supported the tenant-repair ballot question. Sided with the majority on 11 of 13 split votes.
approach: Bring any request for public incentives with clear performance and community-benefit terms; the ForwardEdge denial shows scrutiny of grant extensions. Engage her on economic development as investment with measurable returns for neighborhoods.
engage_on: Economic development with accountability, downtown and corridor projects (Seventh Place Mall), housing, workforce programs.
lead_with: "Equity is the lens" and "Quality of life matters."
cautions: Unlikely to back incentives or deregulation framed only as business relief. Her positions on most Chamber priorities are NOT AVAILABLE from the minutes beyond these votes.

record: Sole nay on three split votes: the McMahon appointment as Planning & Economic Development director, the Western Ave nuisance finding, and the Goodrich Ave zoning appeal; 5 dissents in all. Leads on budget and grants, land use, and events. Moved approval of a Seventh Place Mall final order. Raised concerns about the festival security credit, moved to delay writing off police festival costs, and spoke against the ForwardEdge extension. Spoke in favor of the drive-through ordinance. Sided with the majority on 8 of 13 split votes.
approach: Engage item by item with neighborhood-level impact data. Look for alignment on small business, cultural events and hospitality, and equitable development. Do not count her vote until confirmed.
engage_on: Small-business grants, events and hospitality, land use in her area of focus, budget items.
lead_with: "Quality of life matters" and "Equity is the lens."
cautions: Not reliably in the majority, and her votes least resemble Noecker's and Jost's. Plan coalitions that do not depend on her vote.
